blocks.text: 10.1 How Do Plants Grow?

Plants grow new leaves and branches, thicken their stems and increase in height. Their cells need building materials and energy. Height alone is not a measure of health: a shoot stretched towards light may be taller without becoming sturdy.

Does a plant take ready-made food from soil or make food from surrounding substances? Predict how water and light affect growth, and what evidence would challenge your ideas. Change one condition at a time.

1. Plant similar healthy chilli or tomato seedlings in three matching pots with equal amounts of the same soil. Label A, B and C. Record starting height, leaf number and colour. 2. Keep A in suitable sunlight with moist soil. Keep B in the same light without watering. Keep C in darkness, with soil moisture similar to A. Match temperature and other conditions. 3. Observe at the same time daily for up to two weeks. Measure height from soil level and count leaves consistently. Record actual changes beside your predictions. 4. Stop a treatment if sustained wilting or deterioration occurs; restore suitable light and water and record the date. Do not continue until the plant dies. Use pots with drainage; an adult cuts reused bottles. Avoid waterlogging and overheated boxes. Never taste soil; wash hands afterwards.

pageIllustration.caption: Record growth using the same measurement method.

blocks.text: Record the same measures for each pot

Compare A with B to investigate water availability, and A with C to investigate light. B and C differ in both water and light, so that pair cannot isolate either factor. Suitable light and adequate water usually support continued growth. A plant without water may wilt; one in darkness may become pale and elongated while using stored food. Neither response is guaranteed within a fixed number of days.

blocks.text: The dark-grown plant is tallest, but has a thin stem and pale leaves. Is height alone a sound measure of healthy growth? Use at least two other observations in your answer. A class compares only a watered plant in sunlight with an unwatered plant in darkness. Explain why it cannot tell which difference caused the result. Design a clearer comparison.

The historical text Vrikshayurveda records observations about plants, soil, crop care and manure preparation, including mixtures involving water, barley and pulse seeds. It recognises that planting alone does not ensure flowers and fruit. Such records are part of agricultural history; a particular treatment still needs a fair comparison before we assume that it works in every soil or climate.
10.2 How Do Plants Obtain Food?

Most green plants make carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water using light energy. Roots supply water and mineral nutrients, but minerals are not the plant’s ready-made carbohydrate food. Much of the carbon in new plant material comes from carbon dioxide in air. Animals depend on photosynthetic producers directly or through food chains.

blocks.text: 10.2.1 Leaves and the Starch Test

Many leaves are broad and thin, exposing a large surface to light while keeping internal cells near air spaces and veins. Green tissues contain **chlorophyll**, a pigment that absorbs light used in making food. Leaf shapes vary with habitat; broad leaves are not the only workable design. Some sugars made by a plant are converted into **starch** for storage.

Recall the iodine test from the animal-nutrition chapter. A blue-black colour provides evidence of detectable starch. To see the reaction in a leaf, a teacher first removes much of its green pigment. Testing one leaf for starch does not by itself reveal when, where or under which conditions that starch formed.

Testing one leaf for starch does not by itself reveal when, where or under which conditions that starch formed.

A leaf test is destructive: the same leaf cannot be tested again after a day in light. Comparisons therefore use similar leaves of the same age, from matching plants. Label samples before treatment so they cannot be confused. When comparing patches, use a sketch to preserve their positions. Choose leaves large enough to handle safely, but do not assume that the largest leaf contains the most starch. A photograph or drawing records appearance; iodine supplies a different kind of evidence.

1. Teacher demonstration: soften a suitable leaf briefly in hot water using forceps. Place it in an open boiling tube containing enough ethanol to cover it. 2. Stand the tube in a stable hot-water bath supplied by a kettle or approved electric bath. Wait for much of the pigment to leave. Never heat ethanol directly. 3. With forceps, rinse the leaf in water to soften it. Spread it on a white tile, cover with dilute iodine and observe for a few minutes. 4. Sketch the colour pattern before interpreting it. If unclear, check the iodine against a known starch sample. Teacher handles hot liquids, ethanol, iodine and chemical waste; wear eye protection. Ethanol is highly flammable: keep all flames and ignition sources away. Never taste treated leaves.

Blue-black areas contain starch detectable by this test. An area that remains yellow-brown may contain little or no detectable starch; that is not a measurement of every carbohydrate present. Removing chlorophyll makes the iodine colour easier to distinguish. The treatment prepares a specimen for testing; it is not how a living leaf normally changes colour.

Bhaskar notices leaves with green and cream patches. Such **variegated** leaves offer a comparison within one leaf. He also asks whether light is needed for starch accumulation. Map the patches before removing pigment: testing destroys the original colour guide.

1. Keep two similar watered variegated plants in darkness for about 36–48 hours. A teacher tests a spare leaf: stored starch must fall below detection. Time alone does not guarantee this. 2. Put one plant in suitable light for several hours; keep the other dark. Match temperature, water and exposure time; prevent overheating. 3. Sketch a comparable leaf from each plant. Mark its green and cream patches and light condition before the teacher carries out the same starch test on both. 4. Match each iodine pattern to its original patch map. Record unclear colours too. Restore both plants to suitable growing conditions.
Bhaskar’s reported observations: evidence to interpret

blocks.text: The reported pattern supports a role for both light and chlorophyll in starch accumulation. A cream patch may contain too little chlorophyll to produce detectable starch under these conditions. The test does not prove an absolute absence of chlorophyll. Starch already present before treatment, imported sugars or an unsuccessful test can complicate an explanation.

Red, violet and brown leaves may still contain chlorophyll hidden by other pigments. Their colour alone cannot tell us whether they photosynthesise. Some accessory pigments absorb light used in photosynthesis; others have different roles. A controlled starch investigation is more informative than calling every non-green leaf unable to make food.

Read Bhaskar’s table in two directions. Within the lit leaf, compare green and cream patches: light is shared while pigment differs. Then compare green patches from the lit and dark plants: their colour is similar while light differs. Agreement between these comparisons strengthens an explanation involving both factors. It does not make either comparison perfect. Patches may differ in other tissues, and two plants are not identical. Repeating with more leaves helps show whether the pattern persists.

10.2.2 What Does Air Contribute?

Carbon dioxide is a small part of air. To investigate its role, compare leaves that receive similar light, water and temperature but have different carbon-dioxide availability. **Destarching** means reducing stored starch before a test, usually by keeping the plant in darkness while it continues to use its reserves.

Carbon dioxide is a small part of air. To investigate its role, compare leaves that receive similar light, water and temperature but have different carbon-dioxide availability. **Destarching** means reducing stored starch before a test, usually by keeping the plant in darkness while it continues to use its reserves.

1. Teacher demonstration: prepare two comparable watered plants with starch reduced below detection. Enclose each under an identical transparent bell jar on a plate. 2. Place a stable dish of teacher-prepared sodium hydroxide solution in A, away from plant and soil. Put an equal dish of water in B. Seal both jars to their plates. 3. Give both the same few hours of suitable light. Match plant kind, leaf age, water and temperature; prevent overheating. Sodium hydroxide absorbs carbon dioxide. 4. Test comparable leaves using the same starch procedure. Record iodine colours before interpreting the evidence. Sodium hydroxide is corrosive. Only the teacher handles solutions, jars, hot water, ethanol, iodine and disposal, using eye protection and suitable gloves.

pageIllustration.caption: A clear record helps compare an experiment with its control.

If the control leaf becomes blue-black but the absorber leaf does not, the contrast supports the requirement for carbon dioxide in starch formation. If neither responds, insufficient light, incomplete testing or plant stress may be responsible. If both respond, consider residual starch or leaking seals. A chemical absorber may also change humidity, so repeat and interpret cautiously.

A related arrangement places half of one attached leaf inside a sealed bottle above sodium hydroxide and leaves the other half outside. It compares the two halves after testing. The inside half must not touch the solution. However, bottle shade, humidity and sealing can also differ between halves; a matched enclosure comparison helps examine these alternatives.

Why place a dish in the control jar at all? Both plants should experience an enclosure and similar equipment. Otherwise a result could arise from the jar rather than the absorber. A fair comparison also needs a working positive response: starch in the control leaf shows that the plant and test could produce the expected signal under those conditions. An absorber leaf alone cannot provide that check. A negative result is useful only when we know what the method was capable of detecting.

Does a Lit Plant Release a Gas?

Leaves use materials from their surroundings, but they also release substances. An aquatic plant lets us collect some of the gas that leaves it. Seeing bubbles is evidence that a gas is escaping, not enough to name the gas or measure its purity.

1. Place equal amounts of suitable pondweed under inverted funnels in two beakers. Use equal volumes of the same water. 2. Fill two tubes completely with water. Invert one over each funnel stem, keeping its opening submerged without trapped air. Label A and B. 3. Keep A lit and B dark for the same time at similar temperatures. Record whether gas collects; compare volumes over equal intervals. 4. If enough gas collects, the teacher uses an approved glowing-splint test away from ethanol and other flammables. Learners observe and record without handling fire. Use school-approved pondweed and handle glass safely. Wash hands; never release laboratory pondweed into waterways. If too little gas collects, report that limit rather than inventing a result.

pageIllustration.caption: Plants grow in a range of surroundings.

blocks.text: A glowing splint relighting in the collected gas supports the presence of oxygen-rich gas. Bubbles alone would not establish this. A lit plant may collect more gas than a dark one because photosynthesis produces oxygen, while respiration continues in both. Some oxygen remains dissolved in water or is used by the plant, so collected volume is not its entire production.

A learner sees no bubbles and concludes, “This plant cannot photosynthesise.” Give two reasons the apparatus might show no collected gas even when some photosynthesis occurs. Another learner calls every bubble oxygen. Which extra observation strengthens that claim? Explain why a positive gas test still does not establish that the sample is pure oxygen.
10.2.3 Photosynthesis: Connecting the Evidence

**Photosynthesis** is the process by which green plants use light energy to make carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen. Chlorophyll helps capture the light. Leaves are major sites, but other green parts such as young stems can also photosynthesise. The investigations test parts of this account; no single one demonstrates the whole process.

**Photosynthesis** is the process by which green plants use light energy to make carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen. Chlorophyll helps capture the light. Leaves are major sites, but other green parts such as young stems can also photosynthesise. The investigations test parts of this account; no single one demonstrates the whole process.
Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen

Separate matter from energy as you read the equation. Carbon dioxide and water supply atoms that are rearranged into new substances. Light supplies energy for this process; it is not a substance that roots absorb or a material stored unchanged inside a potato. Some captured energy becomes stored in chemical form. Later, respiration makes part of that energy available for cell activities. The arrow summarises many reactions inside cells, not a single visible mixing step.

Carbon dioxide enters green tissues; roots supply water. Light energy supports food production. The arrows summarise different routes, not hollow pipes through every leaf.

Glucose is a simple carbohydrate. Plants use sugars in respiration and in building other substances, including cellulose in cell walls. They convert some carbohydrate to starch for storage in leaves, roots, stems or seeds. A potato stores starch in an underground stem called a tuber; it does not need to receive sunlight underground to obtain carbohydrate.

blocks.text: A root can grow in darkness because it receives sugars from elsewhere in the plant. These sugars provide both building material and fuel for respiration. The root also needs mineral nutrients and a supply of oxygen. Thus a well-lit shoot cannot solve every root problem: severely waterlogged soil can limit oxygen reaching root cells. Making food, transporting it and using it are linked processes, but success in one does not guarantee that the others work normally.

Rustom Hormusji Dastur (1896–1961) was an Indian plant scientist who investigated photosynthesis, including the influence of water, temperature and light. He led botany at the Royal Institute of Science in Bombay during 1921–1935. His work illustrates why a plant’s response must be studied under stated conditions rather than explained by light alone.
10.2.4 How Do Leaves Exchange Gases?

A leaf looks continuous to the unaided eye. A microscope reveals structures too small to see directly. Examine its surface before explaining how gases enter and leave. Use a teacher-selected leaf that gives a thin, clear peel; not every species is equally suitable.

A microscope enlarges a very small field, not the entire leaf. Examine several fields before describing what is common. Thick or folded tissue may hide pores, while a tear can resemble an opening. A good drawing selects clearly observed structures and records magnification; it does not copy every detail of an ideal diagram. If the preparation is unclear, improve it or examine a prepared slide before concluding that the leaf has no stomata.

1. Teacher demonstration: use forceps to peel a thin piece from the lower surface of a fresh Tradescantia (rhoeo) leaf. Keep it in a watch glass of water. 2. Lay a flat piece in water on a clean slide. Add school-approved stain if needed; lower a coverslip at an angle to reduce trapped air. 3. Start at low microscope power, increasing as directed. Sketch cells and pores; record magnification. Distinguish repeated structures from tears or air bubbles. Handle glass carefully. No learner handles a blade; use prepared slides if necessary. Keep stains away from skin and eyes; wash hands afterwards.
An enlarged interpretive drawing of leaf epidermis. A stoma is a pore bordered by guard cells; the drawing is not a measured micrograph.

The pores are **stomata**; one pore is a **stoma**. Guard cells border each pore and regulate its opening. Gases diffuse between the air and internal leaf spaces. Stomata also allow water vapour to escape. Their distribution differs among plants; many land plants have more on the lower surface, but that is not a rule for every leaf.

The pores are **stomata**; one pore is a **stoma**. Guard cells border each pore and regulate its opening. Gases diffuse between the air and internal leaf spaces. Stomata also allow water vapour to escape. Their distribution differs among plants; many land plants have more on the lower surface, but that is not a rule for every leaf.

Opening stomata can help carbon dioxide enter, but also increases water loss. Closing them conserves water while limiting gas exchange. A leaf does not simply keep every pore fully open all day. Living cells continue to respire even when the pattern of exchange with outside air changes.

10.3 Transport in Plants
Roots take up water and dissolved mineral nutrients. These must reach leaves, developing shoots and other tissues.
10.3.1 Water and Mineral Transport

Unlike an animal’s heart-driven circulation, plant transport uses different structures and mechanisms. A coloured-water comparison can help locate the route taken by water without making the dye itself a nutrient. A cut stem removes roots from the setup: it traces movement through a shoot, but does not test water absorption by roots.

Unlike an animal’s heart-driven circulation, plant transport uses different structures and mechanisms. A coloured-water comparison can help locate the route taken by water without making the dye itself a nutrient. A cut stem removes roots from the setup: it traces movement through a shoot, but does not test water absorption by roots.

1. Fill matching tumblers A and B one-third full with equal water volumes. Add school-approved red food dye to B; leave A colourless. 2. Choose two similar fresh white-flowered carnation or balsam stems. An adult cuts their bases obliquely under water and promptly puts one in each tumbler. 3. Match stem length, leaf area, temperature, light and time. Record starting colours. Next day, describe any coloured regions in stems, leaves or petals. 4. The teacher cuts thin cross-sections above the waterline. Use a hand lens to compare them. Sketch the colour distribution; do not assume the whole stem stains. Adult cutting only. Do not eat flowers or drink dye solutions. Avoid unknown or irritating plant sap; wash hands afterwards.

Coloured regions above the liquid level support upward movement of water containing the dye. Colour may be easier to see in pale petals or a cut stem than in green leaves. No obvious petal colour does not prove that water failed to move: species, dye, exposure time and the cut ends affect the result.

No obvious petal colour does not prove that water failed to move: species, dye, exposure time and the cut ends affect the result.
Illustrative stem tissue after a dye test and an enlarged vascular bundle. Stained water-conducting regions are distinct from the food-conducting tissue; positions vary with plant type.

**Xylem** contains conducting tubes that carry water and dissolved minerals, mainly from roots towards shoots. Evaporation from moist leaf surfaces and loss of water vapour through stomata, called **transpiration**, help draw water upwards through connected columns. Roots supply water to replace what is lost. Plants do not have a hidden pump equivalent to a heart.

Plants do not have a hidden pump equivalent to a heart.
10.3.2 Food Transport

**Phloem** carries dissolved sugars from regions supplying them to regions using or storing them. A mature leaf may supply a growing root, fruit or shoot tip. Flow can therefore be upwards or downwards in different conducting paths; it is not always a one-way journey down from leaves. Starch is converted into soluble substances before stored carbohydrate is transported.

10.4 Do Plants Respire?

A germinating seed can grow before it has green leaves. Its living cells use stored food, releasing usable energy through **respiration**. To look for a product of this process, compare air around germinating seeds with air in a matched control. Darkness prevents photosynthesis from removing carbon dioxide during the comparison.

A germinating seed can grow before it has green leaves. Its living cells use stored food, releasing usable energy through **respiration**. To look for a product of this process, compare air around germinating seeds with air in a matched control. Darkness prevents photosynthesis from removing carbon dioxide during the comparison.

1. Teacher demonstration: germinate overnight-soaked moong beans on moist cotton. Put a small measured sample on damp cotton in flask A. In matching B, use the same cotton and an equal volume of clean glass beads. 2. Keep both dark for a short teacher-selected interval, with plenty of air space. Do not flood the cotton or use mouldy seeds. 3. Fit two-hole stoppers. With separate needle-free syringes, gently draw equal small volumes of headspace air. Briefly open each second tube to admit replacement air; do not draw liquid. 4. Pass equal gas volumes into equal fresh lime-water samples in separate open tubes. Compare initial and final cloudiness; repeat. Record contents, time, volume and observation. Teacher handles glass and alkaline lime water with eye protection. Never suck or blow through reagents or taste seeds. Vent flasks afterwards; avoid prolonged airtight storage.

If the seed flask gives earlier clouding for the same gas volume, the comparison supports additional carbon-dioxide production associated with the germinating seeds. Room air already contains some carbon dioxide, so the control is essential. Microorganisms can also respire; clean, fresh samples reduce that competing explanation. A CO₂ sensor can provide an alternative measurement.

Room air already contains some carbon dioxide, so the control is essential. Microorganisms can also respire; clean, fresh samples reduce that competing explanation. A CO₂ sensor can provide an alternative measurement.

Merely connecting a seed flask to lime water does not ensure that enough gas passes through it to show a change. A test needs a defined gas-transfer step and an open outlet; never pressurise a sealed reagent tube. The comparison detects a product of respiration, not every step of the cellular process.

blocks.text: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water

Living cells in roots, stems, leaves, flowers and germinating seeds respire in light and darkness. Green cells can photosynthesise when conditions permit, and respire at the same time. Saying “plants photosynthesise by day and respire only at night” confuses two processes. Some mature conducting cells are no longer living, so not every cell in a plant respires.

Living cells in roots, stems, leaves, flowers and germinating seeds respire in light and darkness. Green cells can photosynthesise when conditions permit, and respire at the same time. Saying “plants photosynthesise by day and respire only at night” confuses two processes. Some mature conducting cells are no longer living, so not every cell in a plant respires.
Photosynthesis and aerobic respiration

Imagine a short interval in which photosynthesis removes six equal units of carbon dioxide from a leaf’s surroundings and respiration adds two. The surroundings show a net loss of four units, although both processes occurred. These invented numbers illustrate the accounting; they are not measured rates or a fixed ratio. In darkness, photosynthesis stops while respiration continues, so the direction of net carbon-dioxide exchange can change. A measurement of the net effect alone cannot reveal each separate rate.

blocks.text: In bright light, a plant may take in more carbon dioxide than it releases. Does this mean its cells have stopped respiring? Explain the difference between two simultaneous processes and their net effect. At night, a seedling continues growing although it cannot photosynthesise. Trace the stored food and oxygen it uses. Why would keeping its roots waterlogged make the situation different?

Kamala Sohonie (1911–1998) studied plant respiration during her doctoral work at Cambridge. Her research on cytochrome c helped connect energy-releasing processes across organisms. After returning to India, she worked in medical and nutrition research and later led the Institute of Science in Bombay. Her studies of plant foods and the palm sap drink neera linked biochemical research with nutrition.

Think across a whole day, not just one moment. During a favourable light period, a plant may make more carbohydrate than it immediately uses. Some is transported to growing or storage tissues. During darkness, stored carbohydrate helps support continuing respiration and growth. Over longer periods, disease, limited water or poor light can reduce the amount available. This is why a plant’s condition depends on a changing supply and demand for materials, rather than on a simple switch between making food and using it.

Think across a whole day, not just one moment. During a favourable light period, a plant may make more carbohydrate than it immediately uses. Some is transported to growing or storage tissues. During darkness, stored carbohydrate helps support continuing respiration and growth. Over longer periods, disease, limited water or poor light can reduce the amount available. This is why a plant’s condition depends on a changing supply and demand for materials, rather than on a simple switch between making food and using it.

Photosynthesis supplies organic matter and contributes oxygen to ecosystems. Respiration uses food to power living cells and returns carbon dioxide and water. Transport connects these processes within a plant. Their rates do not have to match at every moment: growing plants can store material, and light, water, temperature and other conditions keep changing.

Use your notebook. Support each answer with evidence and explain any uncertainty.

In your notebook, compare photosynthesis and aerobic respiration under four matching headings: raw materials, products, word equation and importance. State the role of light in each and show energy separately from material substances.

Imagine that all organisms carrying out photosynthesis disappeared. Explain likely effects on food supplies, food chains and oxygen over time. Would every stored food supply and all atmospheric oxygen disappear immediately? Give reasons.

A potato slice turns blue-black with iodine. Explain where the carbohydrate was made, how soluble food reached the potato and why finding starch in the tuber does not prove that it photosynthesised underground.
How can a broad, flat leaf help photosynthesis? Give a reason involving light and another involving gas exchange. Explain why leaves in dry environments may have different structures.
Identify X, Y and Z in this summary of aerobic respiration: X + Y → carbon dioxide + Z, with usable energy released. Explain why plants need this process even when they can make their own food.

Krishna grows comparable watered plants in light and darkness. The illustration gives a possible later appearance. (i) What idea could she be testing? (ii) Compare visible traits. (iii) Predict the starch-test results, stating why stored starch and treatment time matter.

Vani starts with comparable destarched, watered plants in four conditions shown below. Assume temperature is suitable and the stated conditions persist. (i) Where would you predict detectable new starch? (ii) Where would you predict little or none? (iii) Where would photosynthesis generate oxygen? (iv) Where would it not? Explain why oxygen collection and production need not be equal.

She compares colours after 2–3 hours. What might she be investigating, and why is D needed? State the light conditions, indicator colour key and other controls needed before predicting results. Use supplied records or a simulation; do not confine animals in classroom tubes.

Design a coloured-water investigation comparing water transport in warm and cool conditions. Specify safe temperatures, matching stems and solutions, what you will measure and repeats. How would changes in humidity, leaf area or airflow complicate the comparison? Do not boil, freeze or heat plants directly.

Explain how photosynthesis and respiration connect food, oxygen and carbon dioxide in nature. Why is “balance” not a claim that every plant always produces exactly as much oxygen as it uses? Include growth and storage in your answer.

blocks.text: Explore Further

With an adult, plant a small humidity-loving plant, such as fittonia or a suitable fern, in a wide transparent jar. Use moist, not waterlogged, compost and bright indirect light. After establishment, fit a lid and record growth and condensation. Open it if overheating, decay or excess moisture develops. Do not use a closed sunny jar for jade or other dry-loving succulents. Survival alone does not measure the separate rates of photosynthesis and respiration.

Choose one local crop. Explain how light capture, respiration and the transport of water, minerals and sugars support its growth and harvestable parts. Investigate one limiting condition, such as dry soil or excessive heat, using reliable agricultural sources. Distinguish evidence from a product’s advertising claim.

Visit a greenhouse with a responsible adult, or interview a grower. Find out how light, water, temperature, ventilation and sometimes carbon dioxide are managed. Compare these conditions with outdoor growing. Do not handle heaters, gas equipment, pesticides or fertiliser solutions; present your observations and questions in a report.
